title: US Army intends to detonate bomb-making material in Iowa on Wednesday despite a court pause. Here’s what we know | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The Justice Department on Sunday asked a federal appeals court to lift its pause on a permit allowing the US Army to detonate nearly five tons of material containing lead azide at an Iowa munitions plant. The Army intends to carry out the detonation Wednesday.

A federal appeals courttemporarily paused the US Environmental Protection Agency permiton Thursday that would allow the Army to detonate the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in tiny Middletown after environmental groups sued. The Army, in coordination with the EPA, plans to destroy nearly 70 drums containing lead azide, acompound used to detonatemunitions, the military branch said. The detonation, originally scheduled for Friday morning, had been moved to Monday, and then Tuesday, before it was later moved to Wednesday.

The Army said Sundayevening that it had moved the detonation to Wednesday “to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced.”

The Army’s plan has drawn heavy pushback from concerned Iowans and politicians about the plume’s spread over a vast swath of Iowa, the Mississippi River and into parts of Illinois. Environmental groups suing the EPA said the Army had, as of late Sunday morning, failed to update the public about latest weather forecasts, as well as projections of the path of the plume containing lead dust. Lead exposure is unhealthy at any level, and it’s especially dangerous to children, health officials said.

The Army said Sunday evening that it was working to safeguard all Americans in the region.

As the legal fight has unfolded, the Justice Department in afilinglate Saturday said the court’s order “does not enjoin or otherwise prohibit the Army from acting under a separate legal authority.” The Army says the degraded material could explode on its own as temperatures drop. “The real choice, in other words, is not between a detonation and no detonation. It is between a planned and mitigated detonation and an unplanned and unmitigated explosion,” the filing said.

Federal officials are now trying to bypass the judicial process and review while not showing they had pursued other safer alternatives than detonation, lawyers representing environmental groups argued.

“People across numerous impacted communities speaking up and demanding accountability is the only reason there was an opportunity to pause and think about better ways to approach the lead azide problem,” Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the environmental groups, said in a statement Sunday.

Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds on Friday activated a state emergency operations center, while officials in nearby Illinois are warning residents about dust spilling over into their state.

The Federal Aviation Administration has restricted flights around Middletown from Monday through Wednesday, according to atemporary flight restriction notice.

Here’s what we know about the planneddetonation and the legal battle.

The Army inMarch, during “routinestockpile surveillance,” discovered lead azide housed in bunkers had been degrading, according to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. Officials evaluating the best way to dispose of the material communicated with “stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed,” Telle said.

The lead azide’s degraded status left it “extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement,” according to an FAQ distributed by the Army to the community last month. “Packing and transporting it poses an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation to personnel handling and transporting as well as to the public.”

After coordinating with the EPA, experts and the community, officials “determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Telle said.

Army officials held an October 15 community meeting to share information about a potential detonation in late November, according todocuments on the plant’s page. Then, on November 15, the community got a notice of a detonation on Friday, according to an Armynews release.

After pushback, theArmy rescheduled the detonationto Monday — the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material,” Telle said.

While noting the court’s pause is still in place, the City of Fort Madisonsaid Saturdayit was notified that the detonation would most likely occur either Monday or Tuesday, but if it doesn’t happen this week, “another time will need to be arranged with additional planning.” City officials said they hadn’t been given any further information but expect the state to issue more details on Sunday.

Waiting too long to detonate the lead azide could pose more hazards later, Telle said. Theemergency permitfrom the EPA would allow the Army to do the detonation between November 13 and February 11, 2027.

Still, the problem should have been evaluated 20 years ago, said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a University of Iowa professor and environmental health expert.

“Somebody left it to rot that long, for it to now being the only option is to blow it up on site because it can’t be moved,” he told CNN.

O’Shaughnessy said the situation is “unprecedented” and called a planned detonation “the lesser of two evils.”

“They’re pretty much up against a wall here to get it done,” he told CNN’s Jessica Dean on Sunday.

The Army had previously awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions, but later canceled the deal citing safety concerns, court filings show, and instead opted to detonate the lead azide. The filings were first reported by The New York Times.

“This decision is supported by the technical consensus across military and federal explosive safety authorities that this is the only safe method of treatment,” read a partially redacted September letter included in the court filings from Amy L. Borman, deputy assistant secretary of the Army for Environment, Safety and Occupational Health.

CNN has reached out to the Army for comment.

Valentine Nzengung, a chief executive at MuniRem, told CNN the Army “told us that they evaluated reports and they found out that controlled detonation was the safest way, and that is why they were moving forward with controlled detonation. They did not provide us much more detail than this.”

Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant have regularly updated officials in Middletown –home to363 people – about the planned detonation, according to Brieanna Beck, the city clerk and municipal officer, who said she has quickly shared each update on the city’s Facebook page. The city has been aware of the detonation plan for a couple of months, she told CNN in an email.

The Army plant sent letters to homes potentially affected by the detonation, Beck said.

The governor’s office and state agencies were coordinating with EPA and Army officials to “continuously monitor the situation and keep local partners informed,” ReynoldssaidFriday.

More than 80 miles north of Middletown, Cedar Rapids is preparing for the detonation. Officials in Iowa’s second-most populous city are taking steps to monitor the drinking water supply —drawn from wells along the Cedar River— for potential contamination, though they don’t anticipate impacts, according to acity update.

But plans and communication around the detonation have gotten strong pushback from environmental advocates, as well as state and federal politicians in Iowa and neighboring Illinois.

Officials in Iowa City, about 60 miles north of Middletown, said they didn’t know about the planned detonation until news began circulating early last week and were unaware of any state or federal agency formally notifying them, according to City Manager Geoff Fruin in a declaration on Saturday supporting the environmental groups’ lawsuit. An email Friday told the city an EPA team was deployed to collect a pre-detonation surface water sample because Iowa City, with a population of over 75,000 people, is within a 100-mile radius of the detonation, he said.

Iowa City officials have been discussing possible protocols to address impacts from the detonation, Fruin said. But he added it’s difficult to plan due to “lack of notice and information.”

Josh Turek, the US senator-elect for Iowa, has called for a delay to the detonation and Rob Sand, the incoming governor, said Iowans’ safety now and in the future should be the government’s top concern.

Parts of western and central Illinois could be affected by the lead plume under the current weather forecast, Illinois state officials said in anupdateFriday. Illinois health and environmental protection officials said they are monitoring the planned detonation and have issued updates to residents.

Illinois agriculture officials haveissued guidanceto protect livestock and pets, recommending keeping animals inside until the plume has passed and warning of exposure through fishing.

Residents should stay indoors on the detonation day, with windows and doors closed for one to two days after as a precaution, Illinois officials said. They also encouraged people to use portable air cleaners equipped with a HEPA filter.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said Friday he had spoken with Telle, urging more transparency about the planned detonation.

Environmental advocates sued the US EPA on Thursday over the emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide, citing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion.

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday temporarily stayed the EPA’s emergency permit until it rules on the groups’ emergency motion, but didn’t say when the court would take action on the case.

The Army, in a joint statement with the US Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA, said Friday afternoon, “The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, is conducted in the safest fashion possible.”

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the statement said, adding they will keep local officials and the public updated.

The cleanup requirements under the current permit are inadequate to properly address the scope and degree of potential impacts, according to Chau, the senior attorney at Earthjustice, who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter.

There doesn’t appear to be sufficient understanding of how far the plume would spread, as well as which bodies of water, such as the Mississippi River, and land would be blanketed with lead dust, including where people live, Chau told reporters Friday.

The Justice Department first cited a federal regulation that exempts responses to an “immediate threat” to human health, public safety, property or the environment from EPA permitting requirements in its Friday filing. In Saturday’s filing, it said the Army intends to invoke that exemption. Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army’s 71st Ordnance Group, which handles explosive ordnance disposal, determined the lead azide poses “an immediate threat,” according to a sworn declaration filed with Saturday’s notice.

The Justice Department has not responded to CNN’s request for comment.

“We want to be absolutely clear that the regulation they cite is an extraordinary and extreme backstop for situations where there is truly nothing else that can be done,” Rachel Rintelmann, a managing attorney at Earthjustice, said in an email of the Friday filing.

Federal courts have the authority to prohibit the detonation, said Richard Revesz, a New York University School of Law professor who specializes in environmental and regulatory law and was an Office of Management and Budget official during the Biden administration.

Courts should carefully consider whether the Army is correct in its assertion that controlled detonation was the “option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area,” Revesz said in an email to CNN, citing Telle’sstatement on the detonation.

There is no safe level of lead in the body, Dr. Sameer Vohra, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, said in astatement. “(And) when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks.”

With the detonation, the hope is if the lead azide spreads over a wider area, it won’t stay in high-level concentrations, according to O’Shaughnessy, the University of Iowa professor.

“It’s kind of like one of these, the solution to pollution is dilution, right?” he said.

There is the potential for exposure through the air during the initial plume or through touch after it has settled, he said.

Lead is toxic to the brain. Exposure is known to cause serious harm to children’s health, resulting in slowed growth and development, as well as problems with learning, behavior, hearing and speech, according to theUS Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Environmental advocates also warn the detonation could worsen health for residents in Iowa, which has thesecond-highest rate of cancer of any US stateand is one of only three states where the rate is rising.

CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report.

CNN’s Holly Yan, Kara Devlin and Bill Kirkos contributed to this report.
